script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: You left a well-paid job in banking to open a bakery. Do you ever regret it?

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: Honestly, there were moments in the first year when I wondered what on earth I'd done. I was working sixteen-hour days and earning a fraction of my old salary.

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: So what kept you going?

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: It sounds like a cliché, but it was the customers. In banking, I never saw the result of my work. Now someone comes in every morning and tells me my bread is the best thing about their day.

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: Would you recommend the same path to others?

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: Only if they've saved enough to survive at least two years without a profit. Passion alone won't pay the rent.

items.question: What does the woman say about her first year?
options: She found it easier than banking.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Today I want to challenge a popular belief: that we only use ten percent of our brains. This idea appears in films and advertisements, but there's absolutely no scientific basis for it.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Brain-imaging studies show that, over the course of a day, virtually every region of the brain is active. Even during sleep, areas responsible for memory and body regulation are working hard.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Moreover, the brain is incredibly expensive to run. It makes up about two percent of our body weight but consumes roughly twenty percent of our energy. From an evolutionary point of view, it simply wouldn't make sense to maintain such a costly organ if ninety percent of it were idle.

items.question: What is the lecturer's main purpose?
options: To promote a new brain-training product
To show that a common belief is false
To explain how films are made
items.explanation: 'Today I want to challenge a popular belief…there's absolutely no scientific basis for it.'

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: Your new novel is set in a future where it never stops raining. Is it a book about climate change?

script.speaker: Author
script.text: People keep asking me that, and I understand why. But for me, the rain was always more of a metaphor.

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: For what?

script.speaker: Author
script.text: For grief. The main character has lost her brother, and the weather reflects her state of mind. Whether the rain is real or not is deliberately left unclear.

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: So you'd be disappointed if readers saw it as an environmental warning?

script.speaker: Author
script.text: Not at all. Once a book is published, it belongs to its readers. If it makes people think about the climate, that's no bad thing.

items.question: What does the author say the rain represents?
items.explanation: '…the rain was always more of a metaphor… For grief.'

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: A recent survey found that young adults are lonelier than any other age group, including the elderly. Dr Ahmed, does that surprise you?

script.text: Not really. People assume that because young people are constantly connected online, they can't be lonely. But loneliness isn't about the number of contacts you have; it's about the quality of your relationships.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: So is social media to blame?

script.speaker: Dr Ahmed
script.text: It's part of the picture, but I'd be careful about blaming it entirely. Young adults also move frequently for study and work, which makes it hard to build lasting friendships. And housing costs mean many live in shared flats with strangers.

It can be cured by going online.
It is caused by having too many friends.
items.explanation: '…loneliness isn't about the number of contacts you have; it's about the quality of your relationships.'

script.speaker: Host
script.text: You've written a book about failure. Why that subject?

script.speaker: Psychologist
script.text: Because we're terrible at talking about it. On social media, everyone shares their successes, so we assume other people fail far less than we do.

script.speaker: Host
script.text: And that has consequences?

script.speaker: Psychologist
script.text: Absolutely. If you believe failure is unusual, you see it as a sign that you're not good enough, so you stop taking risks. But almost every successful person I interviewed for the book had failed repeatedly before they succeeded.

script.speaker: Host
script.text: So what's your advice?

script.speaker: Psychologist
script.text: Treat failure as information, not as a judgement. Ask what it tells you, rather than what it says about you.

items.question: Why does the psychologist think people misunderstand failure?
options: They only see other people's successes.
They fail more often than in the past.
They read too many books about it.
items.explanation: '…everyone shares their successes, so we assume other people fail far less than we do.'

script.speaker: Scientist
script.text: People often ask me whether planting trees can solve climate change. The honest answer is that it helps, but it isn't a substitute for cutting emissions.

script.speaker: Scientist
script.text: For one thing, young trees absorb relatively little carbon; it takes decades before they make a significant difference. For another, planting the wrong species in the wrong place can actually harm local ecosystems, for example by using up scarce water.

script.speaker: Scientist
script.text: Protecting existing forests is usually far more effective than planting new ones. An old-growth forest stores enormous amounts of carbon that would be released if it were cut down.

items.question: What is the scientist's view of tree planting?
options: It is the best solution to climate change.
It is harmful in every case.
It is useful but not enough on its own.
items.explanation: '…it helps, but it isn't a substitute for cutting emissions.'

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: A common piece of study advice is to highlight key points in your textbook. Unfortunately, research suggests this is one of the least effective techniques.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Highlighting feels productive because it's active, but it doesn't require you to process the information deeply. Often, students end up highlighting almost everything.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Far more effective is retrieval practice: closing the book and trying to recall what you've learned, for example by testing yourself with flashcards. It feels harder, and that's precisely why it works. The effort of remembering strengthens the memory.

items.question: Why does highlighting seem useful even though it isn't?
items.explanation: 'Highlighting feels productive because it's active, but it doesn't require you to process the information deeply.'
